title: Episode 209: The Greek Empire: Antiochus Epiphanes, the Abomination of Desolation, and the Maccabean Revolt
description:
Following the death of Alexander the Great, his empire fractured among his warring generals, with Judea trapped as a bloody battleground between the Ptolemies of Egypt and the Seleucids of Syria. In 175 BC, an erratic, megalomaniacal tyrant seized the Seleucid throne: Antiochus IV, who styled himself 'Theos Epiphanes'—God Manifest. Determined to enforce total cultural assimilation across his empire, Antiochus outlawed Jewish religious practices under penalty of death, criminalizing circumcision, Sabbath observance, and Torah study. In December 167 BC, Antiochus committed the ultimate sacrilege: erecting a statue of Zeus Olympus in the Holy of Holies and sacrificing a sow upon the sacred altar of the Temple—an atrocity commemorated as the 'Abomination of Desolation.' In the mountain village of Modi'in, an aged priest named Mattathias refused to sacrifice to pagan idols, launching a fierce guerrilla war led by his brilliant son, Judah Maccabee—'The Hammer.' Routing vast Seleucid armies in the rocky mountain passes, the Maccabees liberated Jerusalem, cleansed the desecrated sanctuary, and witnessed the miracle of the eternal light, giving birth to the festival of Hanukkah.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we witness the epic clash between Greek pagan culture and biblical faith. When an arrogant Seleucid tyrant attempted to erase the law of Moses from the earth, a band of mountain guerrillas struck back with unyielding resolve. Here is George with the story of Antiochus Epiphanes, the Abomination of Desolation, and Judah the Hammer.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE PARTITION OF ALEXANDER'S EMPIRE
When Alexander the Great died in Babylon without an adult heir in 323 BC, his four chief generals—known as the 'Diadochi,' or Successors—plunged the ancient world into four decades of brutal civil war, dividing the empire into four major Hellenistic kingdoms. In Egypt, Ptolemy I Soter established the wealthy Ptolemaic Dynasty ruling from Alexandria, while in Syria and Mesopotamia, Seleucus I Nicator founded the sprawling Seleucid Empire with its capital at Antioch on the Orontes River. Trapped directly between these two rival superpowers, the land of Judea became a geopolitical buffer zone, contested in six successive Syrian Wars. For the first century of Hellenistic rule, under enlightened Ptolemaic control, the Jews enjoyed religious autonomy. In Alexandria, seventy Jewish scholars translated the Hebrew scriptures into Greek, producing the Septuagint. But in 198 BC, at the Battle of Panium near Mount Hermon, the Seleucid King Antiochus III crushed the Ptolemaic armies, annexing Judea into the Seleucid realm and exposing the Jewish people to an aggressive, assimilationist regime. The four-way partition of Alexander's empire fulfilled the precise prophecy in the Book of Daniel concerning the four horns that arose from the great horn. Judea found itself perpetually caught between the Ptolemaic kings of the south and the Seleucid kings of the north.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: ANTIOCHUS IV: THE GOD MANIFEST
In 175 BC, the Seleucid throne was seized by Antiochus III's younger son, Antiochus IV. A hostage in Rome for a decade, Antiochus was a volatile, theatrical megalomaniac who assumed the official royal title 'Theos Epiphanes'—meaning 'God Manifest.' His subjects, noting his erratic antics of dancing naked in the streets and throwing coins into public baths, mocked him behind his back as 'Epimanes'—meaning 'The Madman.' Humiliated in 168 BC on the sands of Egypt by the Roman envoy Popillius Laenas—who famously drew a circle in the sand around the king and demanded a decision before stepping out—Antiochus retreated in bitter fury, determined to forge total cultural uniformity across his fractured empire through radical Hellenization. In Jerusalem, Hellenizing Jewish aristocrats under Jason and Menelaus bribed Antiochus to appoint them High Priest, constructing a Greek gymnasium in the shadow of Mount Moriah where young Jewish men exercised in the nude and wore the broad-brimmed Greek hat of Hermes, provoking deep outrage among the devout population known as the Hasidim. Antiochus IV's volatile personality earned him the derisive nickname 'Epimanes' among his contemporaries. His desperate desire for cultural conformity was fueled by his humiliating confrontation with Roman diplomats on the beach of Eleusis in Egypt.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE ABOMINATION OF DESOLATION: 167 BC
When civil strife erupted in Jerusalem between rival high-priestly factions in 167 BC, Antiochus viewed it as outright rebellion against the crown. Marching on Jerusalem with ruthless fury, his troops slaughtered eighty thousand men, women, and children, looting the royal treasury and the sacred gold vessels of the Temple. Antiochus then issued a draconian royal decree outlawing Judaism: circumcision was punishable by public execution, with mothers who circumcised their infants hanged from the city walls with their babies around their necks; keeping the Sabbath was banned; and possessing a scroll of the Torah was a capital offense, with seized scrolls torn to shreds and burned. On the twenty-fifth day of the Hebrew month of Kislev in 167 BC, Antiochus committed the ultimate sacrilege foretold by the prophet Daniel as the 'Abomination of Desolation': he erected a statue of Olympian Zeus upon the altar of burnt offerings, sacrificed a large female swine upon the sacred stones, sprinkled pig broth throughout the Holy of Holies, and converted the Temple of God into a temple of Zeus. The desecration of the Second Temple in 167 BC was an unprecedented assault on biblical monotheism. Outlawing the Torah, circumcision, and the Sabbath, Antiochus sought nothing less than the total cultural and spiritual eradication of the Jewish people.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE SPARK AT MODI'IN: MATTATHIAS'S CRY
Seleucid military commissioners traveled through the towns of Judea to enforce the pagan decrees, erecting altars and compelling citizens to sacrifice swine and eat unclean meat. In the rocky mountain village of Modi'in, twenty miles northwest of Jerusalem, royal commissioner Apelles assembled the inhabitants, approaching the elderly rural priest Mattathias, of the Hasmonean family: 'Thou art a ruler, and an honorable and great man in this city; come thou first, and fulfill the king's commandment, so shalt thou and thy house be in the number of the king's friends.' Mattathias answered with a roar of unyielding defiance: 'Though all the nations that are under the king's dominion obey him... yet will I and my sons and my brethren walk in the covenant of our fathers! God forbid that we should forsake the law and the ordinances!' When an apostate Jewish man stepped forward to sacrifice upon the pagan altar, Mattathias's wrath burned: seizing a dagger, he struck the apostate down upon the altar, killed the royal commissioner, and tore the altar to the ground. Turning to the villagers, Mattathias shouted: 'Whosoever is zealous of the law, and maintaineth the covenant, let him follow me!' Mattathias and his five sons fled into the Judean wilderness. Mattathias's bold stand at Modi'in echoed the ancient zeal of Phinehas. His refusal to accept royal bribes or compromise his faith inspired a spontaneous rural rebellion that defied the might of the largest Hellenistic military empire in the Near East.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: JUDAH MACCABEE: THE HAMMER IN THE HILLS
When elderly Mattathias died shortly thereafter, leadership of the guerrilla rebellion passed to his third son, Judah, who earned the historic surname 'Maccabee'—derived from the Aramaic word for 'The Hammer.' Operating from the rugged ravines, caves, and mountain ridges of the Judean wilderness, Judah perfected the art of asymmetrical mountain warfare. When the Seleucid general Apollonius marched from Samaria with a large army, Judah ambushed the column in a narrow pass, killing Apollonius, routing the troops, and taking Apollonius's own sword, which Judah wielded in battle for the rest of his life. At the Pass of Beth Horon, when his hungry, exhausted fighters saw the massive Syrian army approaching and trembled, Judah rallied them with words of unshakeable faith: 'With the God of heaven it is all one, to deliver with a great multitude, or a small company: for the victory of battle standeth not in the multitude of an host; but strength cometh from heaven!' Judah struck like a thunderbolt, routing the Seleucids down the rocky gorge. At Emmaus, Judah executed a daring night march, burning the enemy camp while the Syrian generals were searching for him in the mountains. Judah Maccabee's military genius lay in his mastery of terrain and psychological morale. Utilizing the narrow defiles of Beth Horon and the rocky hills of Emmaus, Judah consistently outmaneuvered Seleucid phalanxes that relied on flat, open terrain.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE CLEANSING OF THE SANCTUARY AND HANUKKAH
Having shattered four professional Seleucid armies, Judah and his victorious freedom fighters marched up Mount Moriah to Jerusalem in the winter of 164 BC. Entering the Temple courts, they wept aloud: the gates were burned, weeds grew tall in the courtyards as in a forest, and the altar was polluted by pagan swine. Tearing their clothes, the priests dismantled the defiled altar stones, storing them in a chamber on the temple mount until a prophet should arise to tell what to do with them. They constructed a new altar of unhewn stones according to the Torah, manufactured new golden vessels, repaired the sanctuary, and hung new tapestries. Exactly three years to the day after Antiochus had desecrated the altar—on the twenty-fifth of Kislev, 164 BC—the priests offered the morning burnt offering on the new altar. According to the ancient Talmudic tradition preserved in the Tractate Shabbat, when the priests prepared to light the seven-branched golden Menorah, they could find only a single small jar of consecrated olive oil sealed with the High Priest's signet ring, containing enough oil for only one day. Miraculously, the oil burned continuously for eight full days, until new consecrated oil could be pressed and prepared. Judah and the entire assembly decreed that the days of the dedication of the altar should be celebrated annually with joy and mirth for eight days: the festival of Hanukkah, the Festival of Lights. The rededication of the Temple in 164 BC rekindled the spiritual heart of the Jewish nation. The eight-day celebration of Hanukkah commemorated not only the miracle of the holy oil, but the triumphant preservation of monotheism against pagan tyranny.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE HASMONEAN KINGDOM AND THE SHADOW OF ROME
The miraculous triumph of the Maccabees birthed an independent Jewish state for the first time since the Babylonian exile: the Hasmonean Dynasty. Judah Maccabee fell heroically in battle at Elasa in 160 BC, but his brothers Jonathan and Simon consolidated political independence, fortifying Jerusalem, expanding territorial borders across Galilee, Samaria, and Idumea, and securing formal recognition from the Roman Senate. Yet over the succeeding century, the Hasmonean rulers succumbed to the very corruptions they had fought against: adopting Hellenistic titles, combining the sacred priesthood with royal secular kingship, and engaging in fratricidal dynastic civil wars. When rival Hasmonean brothers Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II fought over the throne in 63 BC, both foolishly invited Roman intervention. Roman general Pompey the Great marched into Jerusalem, besieged the Temple mount for three months, and breached the sanctuary. Pompey walked into the Holy of Holies, astonished to find no physical idol, only an empty room. Judea had traded the Greek yoke for the iron grip of Rome, setting the stage for the final chapter of ancient empire. The Hasmonean state founded by the Maccabees endured for over a century, restoring Jewish sovereignty. Yet internal power struggles and worldly ambition eventually weakened the dynasty, leaving Jerusalem vulnerable to the iron legions of the Roman Republic.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The Maccabean Hammer liberated the Temple and rekindled the sacred Menorah, proving that faith could conquer imperial tyranny. But as the Greek era faded, the iron legs of Nebuchadnezzar's statue stepped onto the soil of Judea: The Roman Empire. Next week, we begin our two-part Roman finale with Episode 210: The Pax Romana, Julius Caesar, Augustus, and the Census of Quirinius: the fall of the Roman Republic, the legions of Caesar, the monumental palaces of Herod the Great, the imperial census that moved an empire, and the birth in Bethlehem. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
